## Q1
Consider the following C program :

```
#include<stdio.h>
int main() {
int x[] = {2,4,6,8,10};
int a, b=0, *y=x+4;
for( a=0; a<5; a++) {
b = b +(*y-a) - *(y-a);
}
printf("%d\n",b);
return 0;
}
What will be the output of the above C program
?
```

## Q1 - Options
(A) 4
(B) 6
(C) 8
(D) 10

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q12

y points at x[4] = 10, and \*y stays 10 throughout. Each iteration adds (10 − a) − x[4−a]: for a = 0 to 4 that is 10−10 = 0, 9−8 = 1, 8−6 = 2, 7−4 = 3 and 6−2 = 4. The running total is 0+1+2+3+4 = 10, so the program prints 10 — option D.

## Q2
Which of the following are TRUE about constructors in C++ ?<br>
A. A constructor can be overloaded.<br>
B. A constructor does not have a return type.<br>
C. A constructor must be declared as a friend function.<br>
D. A constructor is called when an object is destroyed.

## Q2 - Options
(A) (B), (C), (D) Only
(B) (B), (C) Only
(C) (A), (B), (C) Only
(D) (A), (B) Only

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q23

(A) is true — constructors can be overloaded on their parameter lists. (B) is true — a constructor has no return type, not even void. (C) is false: a constructor is an ordinary member function and is never required to be a friend. (D) is false: destruction invokes the destructor, not the constructor. Only (A) and (B), so option D.

## Q3
```
#include<stdio.h>
void f1(char *x, char *y) {
char *t1;
t1 = x;
x = y;
y = t1;
}
void f2(char **x, char **y) {
char *t1;
t1 = *x;
*x = *y;
*y = t1;
}
int main() {
char *a = "ONE", *b = "TWO";
f1(a, b);
printf("%s %s ", a, b);
f2(&a, &b);
printf("%s %s", a, b);
return 0;
}
```

What is the output of the program?

## Q3 - Options
(A) ONE TWO TWO ONE
(B) TWO ONE ONE TWO
(C) ONE TWO ONE TWO
(D) TWO ONE TWO ONE

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q27

f1 receives copies of the two pointers, so swapping them inside the function leaves a and b untouched and the first printf prints ONE TWO. f2 receives the addresses of a and b, so swapping \*x and \*y rewrites the caller’s own pointers and the second printf prints TWO ONE. The full output is ONE TWO TWO ONE — option A.

## Q17
What will be the output of the following code?

```
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
 int a, b, c;
 a = 0x10;
 b = 010;
 c = a + b;
 printf("%d", c);
 return 0;
}
```

## Q17 - Options
(A) 20
(B) 24
(C) Garbage
(D) error

## Q17 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q9

C interprets a leading `0x` as a hexadecimal literal and a leading `0` as an octal literal, so both variables here hold different decimal values than their digits suggest.

`a = 0x10` is hexadecimal 10, which equals 16 in decimal.

`b = 010` is octal 10, which equals 8 in decimal.

`c = a + b = 16 + 8 = 24`, and `printf("%d", c)` prints this decimal value directly.

- **A. 20** — would only follow from treating both literals as decimal, ignoring the `0x` and leading-zero prefixes.
- **B. 24** — correct, from 16 + 8.
- **C. Garbage** — the code has no undefined behavior, both variables are assigned valid literal values.
- **D. error** — the program is syntactically valid and compiles without any error.

## Q18
What is the output of the following code?

```
int main() {
 struct s1 {
  char *z;
  int i;
  struct s1 *p;
 };
 static struct s1 a[] = {
  {"Nagpur", 1, a + 1},
  {"Raipur", 2, a + 2},
  {"Kanpur", 3, a}
 };
 struct s1 *ptr = a;
 printf("%s %s %s\n", a[0].z, ptr->z, a[2].p->z);
 return 0;
}
```

## Q18 - Options
(A) Nagpur Raipur Kanpur
(B) Nagpur Nagpur Nagpur
(C) Kanpur Kanpur Kanpur
(D) Error

## Q18 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q10

Each element of array `a` is a struct containing a name, an integer, and a pointer to another struct in the same array, so tracing the pointers requires following which array index each `p` field actually points to.

`a[0].z` is `"Nagpur"`, the string stored directly in the first element.

`ptr` is initialized to `a`, which is the same address as `a[0]`, so `ptr->z` is also `a[0].z`, which is `"Nagpur"`.

`a[2].p` is initialized to `a`, the address of `a[0]`, so `a[2].p->z` dereferences back to `a[0].z`, again `"Nagpur"`.

- **A. Nagpur Raipur Kanpur** — would only hold if each printed value came from a different array index, but `ptr` and `a[2].p` both resolve back to `a[0]`.
- **B. Nagpur Nagpur Nagpur** — correct, because `a[0].z`, `ptr->z`, and `a[2].p->z` all trace back to the same struct, `a[0]`.
- **C. Kanpur Kanpur Kanpur** — would require all three expressions to resolve to `a[2]`, but only `a[2].z` itself is `"Kanpur"`, not the pointer-dereferenced values used here.
- **D. Error** — the program is syntactically valid, and the self-referential array initialization is legal because `a` is already declared by the time its own elements are initialized with pointers into it.

## Q19
How will you free the memory allocated by the following program?

```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#define MAXROW 3
#define MAXCOL 4
int main()
{
 int **p, i, j;
 p = (int **)malloc(MAXROW * sizeof(int*));
 return 0;
}
```

## Q19 - Options
(A) memfree (int p);
(B) dealloc (p);
(C) malloc (p, 0);
(D) free (p);

## Q19 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q14

Memory obtained through `malloc` in C is released with the standard library function `free`, which takes the pointer returned by the allocation call.

- **A. memfree (int p)** — not a standard C library function.
- **B. dealloc (p)** — not a standard C library function either.
- **C. malloc (p, 0)** — `malloc` only allocates memory and takes a single size argument, it is never used to release memory.
- **D. free (p)** — correct. `free` is the standard C function that releases memory previously allocated by `malloc`, `calloc`, or `realloc`.

## Q20
What is the output of the following code?

```
main ( )
{
 static float a [ ] = {13.24, 1.5, 4.5, 5.4, 3.5};
 float *j, *k;
 j = a;
 k = a + 4;
 j = j * 2;
 k = k/2;
 printf("%f %f", *j, *k);
}
```

## Q20 - Options
(A) 13.25, 4.5
(B) 1.5, 3.5
(C) 13.24, 1.5, 4.5, 5.4, 3.5
(D) Illegal use of pointer in main function

## Q20 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q73

In standard C, pointer arithmetic only permits adding or subtracting an integer from a pointer, or subtracting two pointers of the same type — it does not permit multiplying or dividing a pointer by a number. The lines `j = j * 2` and `k = k / 2` apply `*` and `/` directly to the pointer variables `j` and `k`, which are not valid pointer operations in C.

A standards-conforming C compiler rejects both lines with a type error such as "invalid operands to binary \* (have 'float \*' and 'int')", so the program never successfully compiles and no output is produced.

- **A. 13.25, 4.5** — assumes the pointer arithmetic silently executes and produces a numeric result, which a real compiler would reject.
- **B. 1.5, 3.5** — also assumes valid execution of illegal pointer arithmetic.
- **C. 13.24, 1.5, 4.5, 5.4, 3.5** — assumes the whole array prints, which does not follow from this code even if it compiled.
- **D. Illegal use of pointer in main function** — correct. Multiplying or dividing a pointer by a scalar is not legal C, so the code fails to compile.

## Q21
What is the type of x in the following program?

```
#include <stdio.h>
int main()
{
    typedef (*(*arrfptr[3])())[10];
    arrfptr x;
    return 0;
}
```

## Q21 - Options
(A) x is a pointer
(B) x is a array of three pointer
(C) x is an array of three function pointer
(D) Error in x declaration

## Q21 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q99

Reading the declarator `(*(*arrfptr[3])())[10]` from the identifier outward, with `[]` binding tighter than unary `*` at each step, resolves x's type layer by layer:

- `arrfptr[3]` — arrfptr is an array of 3 elements.
- `(*arrfptr[3])` — each of those 3 elements is a pointer.
- `(*arrfptr[3])()` — each pointer points to a function taking no arguments.
- `*(*arrfptr[3])()` — each such function returns a pointer.
- `(*(*arrfptr[3])())[10]` — that returned pointer points to an array of 10 elements.

So x is an array of 3 pointers to functions, where each function returns a pointer to an array of 10 elements.

- **A. x is a pointer** — wrong. arrfptr is declared as an array, not a single pointer, so x itself is not a pointer.
- **B. x is a array of three pointer** — wrong. This captures the array-of-three-pointers layer correctly but drops that each pointer specifically targets a function, so it under-describes the type.
- **C. x is an array of three function pointer** — correct. It is the only option that names both the array-of-three structure and the function-pointer nature of its elements.
- **D. Error in x declaration** — wrong. The declarator is syntactically valid C, so it does not produce a declaration error.

Among the given options, C is the closest full match to the derived type, so it is the intended answer.

## Q22
Given

int arr[3][4][2] = {{{2,4},{7,8},{3,4},{5,6}},{{7,6},{3,4},{5,3},{2,3}},{{8,9},{7,2},{3,4},{5,1}}};

Which one of the following can be used to refer to element 1 in the above 3-d array?

## Q22 - Options
(A) arr[3][4][2]
(B) *(*(\*(arr+2)+3)+1)
(C) \*(arr+2) + \*(arr+3) + \*(arr+1)
(D) arr[2][3][2]

## Q22 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q10

The value 1 appears only once in the array, inside the innermost pair {5,1} at arr[2][3], so the target element is arr[2][3][1].

*(*(\*(arr+2)+3)+1) dereferences arr+2 to reach the third 2-D block, then +3 to reach its fourth row {5,1}, then +1 to reach the second element of that row, which is exactly arr[2][3][1] = 1

- **A. arr[3][4][2]** — indexes one past the valid range in every dimension, since the declared sizes only allow indices up to 2, 3, and 1.
- **B. *(*(\*(arr+2)+3)+1)** — correct. Reaches arr[2][3][1], the position holding the value 1.
- \*\*C. \*(arr+2) + *(arr+3) + *(arr+1)** — adds three pointer-typed row addresses together instead of dereferencing them, which is not valid element access.
- **D. arr[2][3][2]** — uses index 2 on the innermost dimension, whose declared size is only 2, so valid indices only go up to 1.

## Q23
Allowing different derived classes to be used interchangeably through the interface provided by a common base class is called \_\_\_\_\_\_.

## Q23 - Options
(A) Derived polymorphism
(B) Compile time polymorphism
(C) Static polymorphism
(D) Run time polymorphism

## Q23 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q11

When a program calls a virtual function through a base class pointer or reference, the actual derived-class implementation that runs is decided while the program is executing, based on the real object type behind that pointer.

This late binding of the interface to different derived-class behaviors is exactly what run time polymorphism means, letting derived classes stand in for the base class interchangeably at runtime.

Compile time (static) polymorphism instead covers function overloading and templates, where the exact function is fixed at compile time, so those terms do not describe interchangeable derived-class substitution.

## Q24
Inheritance provides the benefits of \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

A. shared interfaces<br>
B. run-time polymorphism<br>
C. less redundant information<br>
D. dynamic binding

Choose the Correct answer from the options given below:

## Q24 - Options
(A) A, B, C only
(B) A, B, D only
(C) B, C, D only
(D) A, C, D only

## Q24 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q45

Inheritance lets derived classes share a common base class interface, and that shared interface is what makes dynamic binding of overridden operations to their runtime types meaningful, which in turn is what produces run-time polymorphism.

- **A. shared interfaces** — correct. A base class interface is exactly what derived classes inherit and share.
- **B. run-time polymorphism** — correct. Late binding through the shared interface is what lets derived classes substitute for the base class at runtime.
- **C. less redundant information** — more accurately a benefit of code reuse in general, not of inheritance's structural mechanism specifically. A deep or poorly designed hierarchy does not automatically reduce redundancy and can increase coupling instead.
- **D. dynamic binding** — correct. It is the mechanism that ties an overridden operation to the object's actual runtime type.

Because different course references group these four benefits differently, this item is worth checking against the specific textbook list used in the course.
